catalog_quote: Nez Perce and Sahaptin are syllable timed languages with three levels of stress. The orthographic traditions of both languages mark only primary stress with a secondary stress being considered more or less predictable. In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress. Some Nez Perce words also have morpheme inherent stress, which generally is the same as for the Sahaptin cognate. ... For Nez Perce words without inherent stress, the stress is on the penultimate vowel if the word ends in a vowel or single consonant. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical: every root/lexical morpheme carries its own inherent stress on an unpredictable syllable, and some affixes are inherently stressed; in a complex word a single primary stress surfaces on the highest-ranked stressed morpheme (stressed suffix beats stressed prefix beats root). No positional default (contrast Nez Perce penult rule, Rude 2006:272).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rude 2012: three levels of stress, secondary 'considered more or less predictable', not described. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet): in the 'Umatilla reservation dialects' (Umatilla, Walla Walla) 'there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle.. the rules for stress in these dialects are quite elaborate', versus one accent per word in NW Sahaptin; Hargus & Beavert 2014 fn.16 report Rude (1988) suggesting secondary stresses in Sahaptin.
new_statements.exceptions: Function words/clitics unstressed (Jacobs 1931:117: connective ku- and pronominal enclitics never stressed; Hargus & Beavert for Yakima). Hargus & Beavert (Yakima) add 'strong roots' that keep stress against prefixes; not stated for NE.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in citation/orthographic forms (acute accent); statement is for Sahaptin as a whole (all three dialect clusters), with Umatilla as the default source of examples and NE (Walla Walla) forms cited alongside; no NE-specific stress rule is given.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Rude 2012) is made for Sahaptin as a whole -- Rude defines Sahaptin as three dialect clusters incl. Northeast (Priest Rapids/Wanapam, Walla Walla, Palouse) and credits a Walla Walla speaker (Elizabeth Wocatsie Jones) for the NE forms, but his default examples are Umatilla (umat1237, Columbia River Sahaptin). No NE-specific (wall1238) stress description could be opened. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet only) treats Walla Walla together with Umatilla as the 'Umatilla reservation dialects', which he says differ prosodically from NW Sahaptin (yaki1237 etc.) in allowing several gentle accents per word. All detailed modern stress work (Hargus & Beavert; Jansen 2010) is on Yakima = Northwest Sahaptin.

new_statements.quote: [p. 117] "In the Umatilla reservation dialects there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle, with only slightly higher tone; the rules for stress in these dialects are quite elaborate." [p. 118] "In walu'la-palu's, stress is given to all roots and all sorts of morphologic elements that may or may not take word stress in northwest Sahaptin." [p. 120] "It may be, however, that one of the essential accentual drifts in the walu'la-palu's verb has been towards the penultimate syllable, in addition to the general Sahaptin accentuation of root syllables, one root in northwest Sahaptin, one or more than one in walu'la-palu-'s."

In walu'la…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing morpheme-inherent / lexical reading (Rude 2012: 'In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress'): Jacobs likewise makes stress a property of roots and specific affixes rather than of syllable position, and adds detail: several accents per word in NE Sahaptin, the suffix-cluster next-to-last rule, multiple-root stressing, stressable enclitics, and a hypothesised penultimate drift. Not a contradiction of type; it differs from Rude only in describing 2-4 near-equal gentle accents rather than three ranked levels with one primary.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For walu'la-palu's (Walla Walla-Palouse = Northeast Sahaptin) Jacobs describes stress as morphologically assigned: every root and many affixes carry an accent, so a word may have two to four gentle accents (stress and high tone being one phenomenon); verb aspect and tense suffixes are stressed when followed by a suffix or enclitic, and in a cluster of aspect/tense suffixes the next-to-last element takes the stress (-xa'na, -ca'na); when several verb roots co-occur each is stressed unless -ca', -xa', -t'a' or a directional suffix is penultimate, in which case only the first root is stressed; enclitics may be stressed (cala'wica-'c); nouns, pronouns and adverbs follow the northwest-Sahaptin affix-based rules (certain post-positions always stressed, prefixed i'- always accented, otherwise the root's first syllable). Jacobs adds the hypothesis that the walu'la-palu's verb has drifted toward penultimate accent ('Evidences of penultimate accents are numerous.. they occur if the final syllable be unaccented') and says the full verb-stress rules were not supplied.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jacobs does not use a primary/secondary distinction for the Umatilla-reservation (NE) dialects: 'two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle, with only slightly higher tone' (p. 117), contrasted with northwest Sahaptin where 'ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress'. Verb prosody of walu'la-palu's is 'less heavily swinging, more softly singsong' (pp. 120-121); 'Stress accent is gentler, subtler, more difficult for strangers, on Umatilla reservation' (p. 99).
new_statements.exceptions: Connective ku- is never stressed; in northwest Sahaptin pronominal enclitics never take word stress, but 'In walu'la-palu-'s enclitics may receive stress' (p. 121); anterior root -qala- 'roll' is almost never accented (accent goes to the following root element); -Da'xna is stressed only if not followed by a suffix or enclitic; Palouse alone shows a 'peculiar and rather infrequent final verb past tense -ya' accentuation' (p. 119, cross-referenced to vowel elision p. 111); 'We will not note minor stress divergences' (p. 121).
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs's 'walu'la-palu's' is Walla Walla-Palouse, one of his 'Umatilla reservation dialects' (with yumati'la = Umatilla), recorded from Umatilla-reservation speakers in 1930 (walu'la notes from Wade Minthorn); this is Northeast Sahaptin, wall1238. Jacobs's unlabelled or 'northwest Sahaptin' statements (one accent per word, no secondary stress, strong high tone) describe the Yakima-reservation group (Klikitat, Upper Cowlitz, Yakima; yaki1237) and are not statements about wall1238; only the sentences explicitly about walu'la-palu's or the Umatilla reservation dialects/bands were used here. Jacobs also notes a Palouse-only final past-tense -ya' accentuation distinguishing palu's from walu'la.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction of type: Jacobs 1931 (walu'la-palu's = Walla Walla-Palouse) and the catalog's existing statement (Rude 2012, morpheme-inherent stress with a suffix > prefix > root hierarchy, NE data from a Walla Walla speaker) both make stress a property of morphemes rather than of syllable position. They differ in description: Jacobs reports two to four gentle, roughly equal accents per word with no secondary-stress hierarchy in the Umatilla-reservation dialects, whereas Rude describes three levels with one orthographically marked primary stress; Jacobs's hypothesis of a drift toward penultimate accent in the walu'la-palu's verb has no counterpart in Rude. Jacobs's text was obtained only as chained full-text-search snippets (scanned), not page images, so wording and page anchors carry that caveat.
